content_html:
The interest rate on a loan tells you only part of what it costs. Origination fees, discount points and other finance charges add to the price of borrowing, and the annual percentage rate (APR) is the single figure that folds them in. This APR calculator works out the true APR of a fixed-rate loan from the loan amount, interest rate, term and fees, along with the monthly payment, the amount financed and the total finance charge.

How to use this calculator

  1. Loan amount: the amount you are borrowing, before any fees are taken out.
  2. Interest rate: the note rate your payment is based on.
  3. Loan term: years plus any extra months.
  4. Fees paid upfront: finance charges you pay at closing or that the lender deducts from the money it sends you, such as origination, underwriting, processing or application fees.
  5. More options: discount points (each point is 1% of the loan amount) and any fees added to the loan balance instead of paid in cash.

Include only charges that are a cost of credit. Costs you would pay even in a cash purchase, such as an appraisal, title insurance or recording fees on a mortgage, are generally left out of the APR under federal rules.

How the APR is calculated

The calculator follows the actuarial method used for Truth in Lending disclosures:

  1. Work out the monthly payment on the loan balance at the note rate, using M = B × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)−n), where i is the rate divided by 12 and n the number of months. Fees added to the loan are part of the balance B.
  2. Find the amount financed: the loan amount minus fees and points paid upfront. This is the credit you actually receive.
  3. Find the monthly rate at which the payments are worth exactly the amount financed. There is no formula for this, so the calculator narrows it down by repeated halving until it is accurate to far less than 0.001%.
  4. Multiply that monthly rate by 12 to get the APR.

The finance charge is everything you pay beyond the amount financed: total interest plus all fees and points.

Worked example

A $250,000 loan at 6.5% for 30 years with $4,000 of upfront fees:

  • Monthly payment: $1,580.17, for total payments of $568,861.22.
  • Amount financed: $250,000 − $4,000 = $246,000.
  • APR: 6.656%, about 0.16 percentage points above the note rate.
  • Finance charge: $568,861.22 − $246,000 = $322,861.22.

Adding one discount point ($2,500) on top of the fees, without any rate reduction, lifts the APR to 6.755%. The same $4,000 in fees weighs more heavily on a shorter loan, because it is spread over fewer payments:

Limits of the APR

  • The APR assumes you keep the loan for its full term. If you sell, refinance or repay early, upfront fees are spread over fewer years and your real cost of borrowing is higher than the APR suggests.
  • For adjustable-rate loans, the disclosed APR is based on assumptions about future rates and can differ from what you end up paying.
  • APR is not the same as APY. APR is a simple annual rate (the monthly rate × 12); the effective annual rate shown in the results includes monthly compounding and is slightly higher.
  • Mortgage insurance and some lender-specific charges can also count toward an official APR. Your Loan Estimate or Truth in Lending disclosure shows the lender's own figure.

faq.question: What is the difference between the interest rate and the APR?
faq.answer: The interest rate sets your monthly payment. The APR is a broader measure that also counts fees and points, expressed as a yearly rate, so it is usually a little higher than the interest rate.

faq.question: Which fees are included in the APR?
faq.answer: Charges you pay to get the credit, such as origination fees, discount points, underwriting or processing fees and, for many mortgages, mortgage insurance. Fees you would pay in a cash deal, such as appraisal, title and recording fees on a mortgage, are generally excluded.

faq.question: Can the APR be lower than the interest rate?
faq.answer: Rarely. It can happen when the lender gives you credits that more than cover the fees, for example a lender credit at closing in exchange for a higher rate.

faq.question: Is a lower APR always the better loan?
faq.answer: Not always. The APR assumes you keep the loan for the full term. If you expect to repay or refinance within a few years, a loan with lower upfront fees can cost less even if its APR is slightly higher.

faq.question: Why does my lender's APR differ slightly from this result?
faq.answer: Lenders include every finance charge required by regulation, may count odd first-period interest, and follow specific rounding rules. Enter all of the finance charges from your disclosure to get close to their figure.
